behavioral_notes.observation: The transaction lifecycle is a guarded state machine implemented in _update_state: each target state declares allowed source states (e.g. 'done' is reachable only from draft/pending/authorized/error; 'authorized' only from draft/pending). Transitions from a disallowed state are refused with a warning log, same-state writes are skipped, and every write stamps last_state_change and resets is_post_processed. _set_done/_set_canceled additionally call _update_source_transaction_state to roll up child capture/void amounts onto the parent. None of this guard logic is visible in metadata.

_process(provider_code, payment_data) is the generic webhook/redirect entry point: it locates the tx via _search_by_reference (extracting the reference from provider data), validates the amount, applies provider updates via _apply_updates (which calls the _set_* methods), and if tx.tokenize and the resulting state is authorized/done it calls _tokenize to mint a payment.token (vaulting provider_ref so future charges run card-not-present). Provider modules override _extract_reference/_apply_updates/_extract_token_values to plug in acquirer-specific payloads.

Because acquirers confirm asynchronously, a cron retries post-processing of any tx with is_post_processed=False for up to 4 days (PayPal verification window), committing per-tx and rolling back on OperationalError. The base _post_process only flags the tx; downstream modules (account_payment, sale) override it to create the account.payment / confirm the sale.order once the payment is done. This decoupled settlement is invisible to metadata.

payment.provider exposes allow_tokenization, capture_manually and support_* selection flags that gate the transaction operations. _send_payment_request (token charge) and _send_capture_request are no-op hooks on the base transaction; the engine creates child capture/void transactions (_capture creates a child tx and calls _send_capture_request, trapping ValidationError into _set_error). The actual acquirer API calls live in provider override modules.

payment_provider.py imports the 'requests' SDK and centralizes outbound HTTP in _send_api_request: it builds URL/headers/auth via hook methods (provider override supplies API keys/secrets), POSTs with a 10s timeout, raises ValidationError on ConnectionError/Timeout/HTTPError, and logs request+response. This is the canonical example of metadata gap #7 — the module talks to external payment acquirers over HTTP with api-key auth, which no Python field/model metadata reveals.

information_flows: outbound: payment_provider._send_api_request -> external acquirer over HTTPS (requests SDK, api-key auth)
side-effect: _tokenize -> creates payment.token from successful authorized/done transaction

external_integrations.pattern: Centralized outbound HTTP in payment.provider._send_api_request; provider-override modules (Stripe, PayPal, Mercado Pago, etc.) supply endpoints, API keys and auth via _build_request_url/_build_request_headers/_build_request_auth hooks. Inbound settlement via acquirer webhooks/redirects to public controllers.
external_integrations.note: Prime example of metadata gap #7: external acquirer communication is invisible to model/field metadata.

value_streams: Collect-Payment: initiate transaction -> redirect/inline to acquirer -> webhook notification -> state machine (done/error) -> post-process settlement
Tokenize: successful transaction -> vault payment.token -> later card-not-present charge via _send_payment_request
organization: (no module-owned res.groups; relies on portal/base account groups and 5 record rules for scoping)
policies: 5 record rules: partner-scoped visibility of own payment.token / payment.transaction (portal self-service)
payment.provider.state (disabled/enabled/test) gates whether a provider can process; test mode runs a fake interface
guarded state machine: _update_state refuses illegal transitions
metrics: payment.transaction pivot/graph (transaction volumes, amounts, state distribution)

classification.apqc_category: 9.0 Manage Financial Resources (9.5 Process payments / collect cash)
classification.rationale: payment is a value-network (Stabell & Fjeldstad mediating-technology) component: its purpose is to interconnect two parties who would not otherwise transact directly — the payer and the merchant/acquirer — by provisioning a mediation service (network promotion & contract management = provider/method onboarding and tokenization; service provisioning = the transaction; infrastructure operation = the requests-based acquirer link and webhook settlement). It does not transform inputs into outputs (chain) nor solve a bespoke customer problem (shop); it brokers a financial exchange across a network of acquirers. We chose 'network' over 'support' deliberately: although it is an infrastructure/engine module (category Hidden, no end-user app) and from the enterprise's value-chain perspective sits in the support activity_class under 9.0 Manage Financial Resources, its own internal logic is mediation, not transformation — hence value_model=network, activity_class=support.

standard_capabilities: provider-agnostic payment flow (redirect, inline, token, express)
asynchronous settlement via webhook + post-processing cron
typical_fits: standard online checkout collecting card payments through a supported acquirer
multi-provider / multi-company provider configuration with test mode
common_gaps: the base engine ships no live acquirer — a payment_<provider> override module is required to actually reach an acquirer
custom acquirer integrations (new provider, regional gateway) need a dedicated module implementing the API/webhook hooks
bespoke post-processing (custom document confirmation beyond account/sale)
